content:
"The passage delves into the enduring yet somewhat outdated notion that 'great men' – individuals esteemed for their talent, bravery, and charisma – have historically steered the course of the world through sheer force of personality. This concept, which gained prominence in the 19th century under thinkers like Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, posits that historical progression is largely dictated by a select few extraordinary figures, such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad. These leaders, in Carlyle's view, possess an almost supernatural ability to influence and transform their surroundings, effectively overshadowing the masses who merely observe and follow.

Despite the emergence of more egalitarian and Marxist social theories, which emphasize the collective agency of the working class, and the historical methodologies of the 1960s that sought to tell history from the perspective of the common people (as championed by historians like E.P. Thompson), the 'great man' theory has shown remarkable resilience. This is partly due to its romantic appeal and the human tendency to venerate powerful individuals.

However, the contemporary iteration of this theory is often more troubling. In the modern era, those who view themselves as 'great men' are frequently far from the heroic figures envisioned by Carlyle. Instead, they are often categorized as anti-heroes or villains. While these individuals may indeed wield significant power, their leadership is characterized by ruthlessness, arrogance, and an unwavering belief in their own infallibility. They impose their will on others, convinced that they possess unique insights and a sacred duty to lead, often to the detriment of those they ostensibly serve. The persistence of this archaic belief system underscores a disconcerting tendency in human society to grant unchecked power to those who claim a special mission or calling, regardless of the harmful consequences that may ensue."
